sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Lono** ​(*lono*) — ‌Agriculture, Peace, ‌Rain · ​Hawaiian deity, ​associated ​with fertility, ​agriculture, rainfall, ​music and ‌peace — ​belongs to ​the ‌Polynesian tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Agriculture, Peace, ​Rain". The ​name means ​"Hawaiian deity, ​associated with ‌fertility, ​agriculture, rainfall, ‌music and ​peace"[^1].

**Lono** ‌is the ​Hawaiian ‌god of ​fertility, agriculture, ‌rainfall, music, ​and peace ​— the ‌deity ‌of the ‌Makahiki season, ​when war ​was forbidden ‌and ​the feathered ​image of ‌the long ​god made ​its circuit ‌of ​every island ‌collecting tribute. ​His name ​is the ​ordinary ​Hawaiian word ‌for news ‌and tidings, ​as if ‌the arriving ​god ​were good ‌news himself.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly ​spelling **Lono** ‌and serves ​its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/lono/). The ‌displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *lono* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters: no ​recovered diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​modern ​Polynesian orthographies; ​macron ​usage ​follows each ‌tradition’s ​reference ​dictionaries. ‌Etymologically the ​name ‌means ​"Hawaiian deity, ‌associated ​with ​fertility, ​agriculture, rainfall, ​music ​and ‌peace"[^1].

The ​canonical ‌spelling ​**Lono** matches ‌the ​conventional ‌scholarly ​romanization. The ‌plain ​ASCII ​form *lono* ‌contains ‌the ‌same ​letters, so ​no ‌lost ​diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition ​is claimed. ​The ‌editorial ​work ‌is to ​fix ​one ​reviewed reference ​spelling, ‌preserve ‌capitalization and ​provenance, ‌and ​keep ​the original ‌evidence ‌visible. ‌The displayed ‌form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed ​form ​itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**l** → ‌**L** ​— ‌Same, capitalized
- ​**o** ‌→ ​**o** ‌— Same
- ‌**n** ​→ ​**n** — ​Same
- ​**o** ‌→ **o** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/lono/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**lono** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Lono.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Lono" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Lono" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"lono" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Lono ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Lono ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous writing ‌system ‌is securely ​attested ​for ​individual polynesian ​names. ​The form ‌shown ​is a ​modern ‌scholarly ​transliteration.[^1]

The ‌form ​**Lono** is ‌therefore ​a scholarly ​transliteration ​rather ​than an ​attested ‌ancient spelling; ​it ‌encodes the ​reconstructed ‌sound ​of the ‌name ​for modern ‌use, ​and no ​mark ‌in ‌it is ‌decorative.

​Hawaiian was ​an ‌unwritten language ​until ​the ‌1820s, when ​mission ​scribes fixed ‌the ​alphabet, so ‌the ​name has ​no ​older ​orthography for ‌canonical ‌to recover ​— ‌Lono is ​itself ​the ‌first spelling. ‌The ‌philological record ‌is ​the sound ‌change ​instead: ​pan-Polynesian ***Rongo** ​becomes ‌Hawaiian **Lono** ​by ​the regular ​shift ‌of ​*R to ​l, ​with the ‌second ​*g dropping, ‌leaving ​a ‌name that ​Hawaiian ‌speakers heard ‌as ​both the ​ancient ​god ​and their ‌own ‌word for ​tidings.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Lono ‌place agriculture, ​peace, ​rain ​at the ​center ​of a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

Lono ​appears ‌in polynesian ​tradition ‌as ​agriculture, peace, ​rain. ​The name's ​meaning, ​"Hawaiian deity, ‌associated ​with fertility, ‌agriculture, ​rainfall, music ‌and ​peace", ‌shapes the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ​figure.

### Worship ‌and ‌Memory (Cult)

‌Devotees ​and later ​tradition-keepers ‌preserved ​Lono in ​ritual, ‌text, and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived into ‌the ​modern scholarly ​record.

​The ​myths of ‌Lono ‌survive in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ​later ​retellings. Each ‌version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of ​its tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and scholars. ‌The ​PuniCodex entry ​does ​not privilege ‌a ​single ​version; it ​gathers ‌the attestations ​so ‌that readers ​can ‌compare them. ​The ‌restoration Lono ‌gives ​the ​figure a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Lono ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Lono, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​agriculture ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Lono ​is the ‌god who ‌comes back ​— and ​that is ​nearly the ​whole of ​him. He ‌does not ​rule from ​a fixed ‌temple; he ​arrives, stays ‌four months, ​and leaves, ‌and the ​year is ​built ​around his ​absence as ​much as ‌his presence. ​In this ‌he is ​almost unique ‌among the ​great gods ‌of the ​world: a ‌deity whose ​defining quality ​is returnability. ‌When Cook ‌sailed in ‌during ​the Makahiki, ​the Hawaiians ‌did not ​need to ​invent anything. ‌Myth had ​already written ​the scene: ‌the god ​lands from ‌across the ​sea, is ​received by ​the chiefs ​and priests, ‌and then ‌— the ​season ‌being over ​— is ​let go. ‌It is ‌among the ‌most honest ‌creations any ​people made ‌of their ​relationship with ​power: the ​blessings arrive ‌seasonally, the ​taxes are ​gathered religiously, ​and the ‌god, ​like rain, ​is trusted ​because he ‌has always ​come back ‌before. To ​live under ‌Lono is ​to live ‌in a ‌world where ​peace has ​a schedule, ​and where ​hope is ‌not optimism ‌but calendrical ​fact.[^1]
